quick_answer: The Rhumb Line Distance Calculator measures the distance along a rhumb line — the constant-compass-bearing path between two coordinates. Enter the endpoints and read the loxodrome distance in kilometres, miles or nautical miles, with the great-circle comparison that shows what steering one steady heading costs over the shortest route.

Why is the rhumb line longer?
It refuses the shortcut. The great circle cuts toward the pole where meridians converge; the rhumb holds its angle and walks the longer, parallel-hugging road.
Yes — divide kilometres by 1.852; a 5,758.6 km Atlantic rhumb is about 3,110 nautical miles. Mariners plan in those units natively.
Barely. Under a few hundred miles at temperate latitudes the two distances agree within a fraction of a percent, which is why coastal work never noticed the difference.
The rhumb follows the parallel itself (a small circle); the great circle dips toward the pole and wins. At 45°N the saving on a long east-west run is the classic textbook result.
Can the rhumb distance be shorter than great circle?
Never — the great circle is the shortest path on a sphere by definition. Any tool claiming otherwise has a bug, and this comparison is how you catch it.
Which should a flight plan use?
Airlines fly great-circle-based routes (in airway segments), because 4% of an ocean is real fuel. Ships balance the saving against weather routing; both start from these two numbers.
